pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7–9; know how rainforest animals are ADAPTED to survive — camouflage (leaf insects, tree frogs), warning colours/aposematism (poison dart frogs), prehensile tails (monkeys), specialised beaks (toucans), nocturnality — and link each feature to the survival job it does.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS2 Y4 'Living things and their habitats' (how animals are suited to their environment) and Y6 'Evolution and inheritance' (adaptation) — the exploratory age-7 seed of the adaptation idea.
• Standards — US: NGSS 3-LS4-3 (organisms survive well/less well in an environment) and 3-LS3-2 / 4-LS1-1 (structures that function for survival).
• Operational details — always pair FEATURE → FUNCTION → SURVIVAL: camouflage hides prey from predators (or predators from prey); bright colours WARN 'I'm toxic, don't eat me'; prehensile tail = a fifth hand for gripping high branches; big light beak reaches distant fruit; nocturnality dodges daytime heat and predators. Tie each to a rainforest LAYER (prehensile tail in the canopy, camouflage on the floor). Contrast camouflage (hide) vs aposematism (advertise) as opposite strategies that both aid survival.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (7): name three adaptations. Tier B (8): explain how each helps the animal survive. Tier C (9): give a specific animal for each, its layer, and contrast why one hides while another shows off.
bestPractices: Always chain FEATURE → FUNCTION → SURVIVAL, never leaving an adaptation as a bare fact ('bright colours' → 'warn predators' → 'so it isn't eaten').
Contrast opposite strategies (camouflage hides vs aposematism advertises) to show both can serve survival.
Tie each adaptation to a rainforest LAYER, reinforcing the layers prerequisite (prehensile tails in the canopy, camouflage on the floor).
Use predict-then-check: ask what happens if the feature is missing/wrong before revealing, to build causal reasoning.
Give a concrete named example per adaptation so the abstraction stays anchored to real animals.
keyRepresentations: Feature→function cards: camouflage=hide, warning colour=deter, prehensile tail=grip, beak=reach food, nocturnal=avoid heat/predators.
A same-animal-two-backgrounds image showing camouflage working vs failing.
A predator's-eye view used to test whether prey is spotted.
A layered rainforest cross-section with each adapted animal placed in its layer.
commonMisconceptions: 'Bright colours help animals hide' — opposite: aposematic colours ADVERTISE toxicity as a warning.
'Animals choose to adapt / decide to change' — adaptations are inherited traits shaped over generations, not a lifetime choice.
'Camouflage means invisible' — it works against the RIGHT background and against a predator's vision, not absolutely.
'A tail is just for balance' — a prehensile tail actively grips like a hand.
'All rainforest animals are active in the day' — many are nocturnal to avoid heat and predators.

learn.summary: Help 7–9 year-olds understand how rainforest animals are adapted to survive, always chaining FEATURE → FUNCTION → SURVIVAL. Cover camouflage (leaf insects, tree frogs hide), warning colours/aposematism (poison dart frogs advertise toxicity), prehensile tails (some monkeys, such as spider and howler monkeys, grip canopy branches with their tails), specialised beaks (toucans reach distant fruit) and nocturnality (often avoiding predators or finding food, and for some animals avoiding daytime heat or drying out). Tie each adaptation to a rainforest layer, and contrast camouflage (hide) against aposematism (advertise) as opposite tricks that both aid survival. The core objective is causal: a feature is not decoration — the right trait in the right layer can make the difference between surviving and not (being eaten, falling, or going hungry).

activities.title: Predator's-eye survival scenarios
feedback: When the dulled dart frog gets attacked: 'Its bright colour was a WARNING, not a mistake — with the colour gone the bird is no longer warned, so it is more likely to attack the frog (and could be poisoned itself). Restore the bright colour and the bird is more likely to avoid it, because many predators learn, or instinctively tend, to avoid bright warning colours — the colour is a warning that helps keep the frog safe.'
When the camouflaged insect is spotted on the wrong background: 'Camouflage only works against the RIGHT background and against a predator's eyes — it does not make an animal invisible everywhere.'
When the tail is removed and the monkey slips: 'A prehensile tail is a fifth hand that actively grips, not just for balance — it lets the monkey hold on high in the canopy.'
If a learner says the animal chose or decided to change: 'Adaptations are inherited traits shaped across many generations — an individual frog cannot decide to turn bright.'
activities.rationale: Adaptation is a feature-consequence relationship best built by predict-then-check: equip an animal with a feature and observe whether it survives, so FEATURE→SURVIVAL becomes causal rather than a stated fact. Optional interaction examples — dragging the leaf insect between backgrounds, a predator's gaze that reveals or misses prey, toggling the frog's colour, and adding/removing the tail with survival recomputed each time — make the mechanism concrete. These are illustrative, not mandatory; the same reasoning works with paper scenes, cut-out animals on different backgrounds, or acted-out role play.
sourceClaims: Camouflage, aposematism (warning colouration in toxic species like poison dart frogs), prehensile tails and specialised beaks are adaptations that improve survival in rainforest animals
learnerActions: Place a leaf-mimic insect onto a bright red flower, then predict whether a hunting bird will spot it; move the same insect onto a matching green leaf and predict again, then check which one the bird is more likely to spot and catch in this scene.

Meet a poison dart frog with blazing blue/red colour; predict what happens if its colour is dulled to try to hide it, then compare with keeping it bright and watch whether the predator approaches or veers away.

Give a spider monkey its prehensile tail and watch it wrap the tail round a high branch to hang and reach for fruit, then remove the tail in the model and see it can no longer hang by its tail, so it must cling with hands and feet and reaching far becomes riskier — connecting the feature to surviving in the canopy.
For each animal, state the FEATURE, the FUNCTION it does, and the SURVIVAL problem it solves, and say which rainforest layer it lives in.
Before each reveal, predict what happens if the feature is missing or wrong (predict-then-check).
activities.intendedInsight: A feature such as colour, tail or beak is not decoration: the right trait in the right layer can make the difference between surviving and not — avoiding being eaten, holding on, or getting food. Hiding (camouflage) and shouting 'I'm poisonous' (aposematism) are opposite tricks doing the very same job — staying alive. Camouflage works against the RIGHT background and a predator's vision, not absolutely.

activities.title: Feature → function reference gallery
feedback: A reveal should give the survival JOB ('bright colours = warning: I'm toxic, don't eat me'), not merely restate the feature.
If a learner treats the tail as only for balance, the reveal should emphasise it actively grips like a hand.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal gallery cleanly delivers each feature→function→layer pairing and works as a reference. Its observable limit is that it STATES the survival benefit rather than letting the child test it, so it is best used alongside, or after, the predict-then-check scenarios.
sourceClaims: Camouflage, aposematism (warning colouration in toxic species like poison dart frogs), prehensile tails and specialised beaks are adaptations that improve survival in rainforest animals
learnerActions: Explore each adapted animal and reveal the survival job its feature does: camouflage = hide, warning colour = deter predators, prehensile tail = grip, big light beak = reach distant fruit, nocturnal = avoid predators and find food (for some, avoid daytime heat).
For each hotspot, note which rainforest layer the animal belongs to (e.g. a spider monkey's prehensile tail in the canopy, a leaf insect camouflaged among understory or canopy leaves).
Use a same-animal-two-backgrounds image to see camouflage working on one background and failing on another.
activities.intendedInsight: Each feature pairs with a specific function and survival benefit, and each animal sits in a particular rainforest layer. This anchors the abstraction to real named animals.

activities.title: Match and contrast end-check
feedback: If a learner marks the dart frog's colour as camouflage: 'Bright colour here ADVERTISES toxicity as a warning — the opposite of camouflage, which hides.'
Reinforce that both hiding and warning are different routes to the same goal of survival.
activities.rationale: Matching and selection questions map directly to the evidence statements and make a tidy final check. They mainly check recall and recognition rather than building the causal feature→survival intuition, so this works best as a check after the scenario and gallery activities. Recognition alone does not elicit independent production of the causal reasoning.
learnerActions: Match each adaptation to the benefit it provides (camouflage→hide, warning colour→deter, prehensile tail→grip, beak→reach food, nocturnal→avoid predators/find food, for some avoid heat).
Answer a contrast question: given a described animal, decide whether it survives by HIDING (camouflage) or by being SEEN (warning colours), and explain why.
Name a specific animal for each adaptation and its rainforest layer.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can distinguish the opposite strategies of hiding versus advertising, and connect real animals to their adaptation, benefit and layer.

activities.title: Explain the dart frog paradox (discussion probe)
feedback: Target answer: the bright colour is a WARNING, not a mistake; it says 'I'm poisonous — don't eat me' so predators learn, or instinctively tend, to avoid it, the opposite of a camouflaged leaf insect or tree frog that hides by blending in.
If the learner can describe a feature but not its survival job, ask 'what problem does this feature solve?' (grip, reach, hide, warn).
activities.rationale: A reasoning prompt that forces the advertise-vs-hide contrast can discriminate the concept child from one holding 'bright colours help hiding': only the concept child can explain why an easy-to-spot frog survives. Asking for a spoken or written explanation elicits the causal reasoning directly, which a matching check does not require. The harmless-bright-frog question edges into Batesian mimicry, so keep it open rather than asserting a definitive answer at this age.
learnerActions: Consider: a poison dart frog is bright, shining red — one of the easiest things to spot in the forest. Explain why a frog would be coloured that way when it makes it so easy to see.
Explain how that is different from a leaf insect's dull, blending colours.
Answer the extension: what will a predator do next time it sees a bright frog after once eating one and getting sick, and how does that protect other frogs?
Discuss: if a harmless frog were also bright red but NOT poisonous, could that still help it? Why?
activities.intendedInsight: Bright warning colour advertises toxicity (aposematism) so predators learn, or instinctively tend, to leave it alone — the opposite strategy to camouflage, which hides. One animal survives by being SEEN, one by being HIDDEN.

constraints: Never leave an adaptation as a bare fact: always chain FEATURE → FUNCTION → SURVIVAL (e.g. 'bright colours' → 'warn predators' → 'so it isn't eaten').
Correct the common misconception that bright colours help an animal hide: aposematic colours ADVERTISE toxicity; contrast explicitly with camouflage.
Camouflage does not mean invisible — it works against the RIGHT background and against a predator's vision, not absolutely. Scenarios should show it both working and failing.
Adaptations are inherited traits shaped over generations, not a lifetime choice an individual makes; avoid language implying a frog 'decided' to turn bright.
A prehensile tail actively grips like a hand; do not reduce it to 'just for balance'.

Note that many rainforest animals are nocturnal — often to avoid predators or find food with less competition, and for some to avoid daytime heat or drying out — countering the assumption that all are active by day.

A reference gallery states benefits and a matching check checks recall; neither on its own elicits the independent causal reasoning of the predict-then-check scenarios or the explanation probe. Use them as complements, not substitutes — this is a narrow affordance limit, not a claim that any one medium is required for understanding.

Interaction examples (dragging, predator's gaze, colour toggle, tail add/remove) are illustrative options; the learning works equally with paper scenes, cut-outs or role play and these mechanisms are not mandatory.
Predator avoidance of warning colours reflects learned and/or innate behaviour toward bright signals generally; do not frame it as one individual bird remembering one specific frog it never ate.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Both cited sources are marked verified:false in the row; treat the DfE curriculum link and NHM adaptation overview as unconfirmed.

The extension question about a harmless but bright frog touches on mimicry (Batesian), which is beyond the stated topic scope; keep it as an open discussion prompt rather than asserting a definitive answer at this age.

The 'predator learns to avoid after getting sick' framing is a reasonable simplification; actual predator learning and innate avoidance vary and were not independently verified here. Activity 1 feedback was reworded so avoidance is attributed to predators generally rather than to one bird remembering one frog.
Activity 3's sourceClaims is [] because the only candidate claim (DfE curriculum standards) supports the topic/necessity, not the activity's recall-check teaching principle.

The NHM claim is retained on activities 1 and 2 because it directly supports the feature→survival relationships those activities teach; its fit with the gallery's method (vs its content) is borderline and flagged.

probeDeeper: How does a prehensile tail help a monkey survive in the canopy?
Why are so many rainforest animals active at night instead of in the hot day?
A predator eats one bright frog and gets sick. What will it do next time it sees a bright frog — and how does that protect other frogs?
What if a harmless frog were also bright red but NOT poisonous — could that still help it? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: The bright colour is a WARNING, not a mistake. It advertises 'I'm poisonous — don't eat me!' (this is called aposematism), so predators learn to leave it alone. That's the opposite of a leaf insect or a well-hidden tree frog, which use camouflage — dull colours and shapes that blend in — to hide. So one animal survives by being SEEN and one by being HIDDEN.

errorPatterns.pattern: bright colours help an animal hide — 'the colours are camouflage'
errorPatterns.nextMove: bright warning colours ADVERTISE toxicity (aposematism); contrast with camouflage, which hides
errorPatterns.distractor: The bright colours help it hide from predators
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the dart frog's bright colour helps it blend in

errorPatterns.pattern: adaptations are just for looks / no survival purpose — can't link a feature to survival
errorPatterns.nextMove: for each feature ask 'what problem does it solve?' (grip, reach, hide, warn)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes a feature but can't say how it helps the animal live

errorPatterns.pattern: an animal chooses its own adaptation — 'the frog turned bright to scare them'
errorPatterns.nextMove: adaptations develop across generations, not by an animal deciding
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes the adaptation as a deliberate choice by the individual

responseLevels.gap: Thinks bright colours are camouflage; can't link features to survival.
responseLevels.full: Explains bright warning colour as advertising toxicity (aposematism), contrasts it with camouflage (hiding), and links at least three adaptations to the survival problem each solves.
responseLevels.partial: Describes several adaptations but treats warning colour as hiding, or names features without the survival reason.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A poison dart frog is bright, shining red — one of the easiest things to spot in the whole forest. If bright colours make it so easy for predators to see, why on earth would a frog be coloured that way? Tell me why, and then tell me how that's different from a leaf insect's colours.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding 'bright colours help hiding' can't explain the dart frog; the concept child sees bright = warning of toxicity (aposematism) as the opposite strategy to camouflage. The reason-tier forces the advertise-vs-hide contrast.
